title: Failure
hook: Peter, Paul, David, Moses all failed badly

segments.voice: Yesterday: God setteth the solitary in families, and from the cross, behold thy mother. Your line was set in families.

A short list of résumés. One man killed someone and fled the country. One took another man's wife, then arranged for the husband to die in battle. One went house to house dragging believers off to prison. One promised he would never deny his friend, and then did, before the cock crowed. Moses. David. Paul. Peter. Scripture writes these moments down in plain sight. And none of their stories stops there.

Peter's story has a strange order. Before the denial, Jesus tells him in Luke: "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." The comeback is spoken before the fall. Then Peter denies him, and "Peter went out, and wept bitterly." Later, by the sea in John's Gospel, the risen Jesus asks him, "Lovest thou me?" and gives him a job: "Feed my sheep." Then David. Nathan the prophet tells him of a rich man who steals a poor man's only lamb. David is furious. Then Nathan says it: "Thou art the man." David answers, "I have sinned against the LORD." The heading of Psalm 51 ties it to this moment: "Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." The story is honest that consequences stay. But it keeps going. Then Moses, whose running you met in year two. He killed a man and ran to Midian. And it was there, keeping someone else's sheep, that the bush burned and the call came. The call found a man who had run. Last, Paul. He never pretends the past didn't happen: "I am the least of the apostles, that am not meet to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God." Then the next sentence: "But by the grace of God I am what I am." Failure is not final doesn't mean failure didn't matter. Peter wept. David's house suffered. But in each story, the failure is a chapter, and the book goes on.
screen: `THE CALL FOUND A MAN WHO RAN.`
`BY THE GRACE OF GOD I AM WHAT I AM.`

segments.voice: Choose one failure you keep replaying, one that still stings, and name it the way Paul named his: this happened, and it was mine. If you can still make it right, set that aside for later; for now, put down the punishment. If you pray, say David's line, create in me a clean heart, O God; if you don't, tell yourself plainly: that was a chapter, not the end. If it ever turns into thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Failure. Falling short, sometimes badly. In scripture Moses, David, Paul and Peter all fail, and every one of their stories keeps going.
Your line: failure is not final. Peter wept, and then was given a job. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians bring their failures to God in confession, privately or in a service, and Catholic and Orthodox Christians also confess to a priest and receive absolution; Psalm 51 is used as a prayer of repentance in several liturgies.

fork.setup: you're Peter. you denied Jesus three times. now the risen Jesus is on the shore asking, lovest thou me? what does he do next?
options: give you a job: feed my sheep.
fork.reveal: he asks, and each time gives Peter work: feed my lambs, feed my sheep. the one who failed is sent to care for others.

original.note: Hebrew: I have sinned — David's answer to Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:13.

chat.says: I really messed up last year. Can someone who failed that badly still be used by God?
options: In scripture, yes: Moses ran, David sinned, Peter denied, Paul persecuted, and each story kept going.
Only small failures; the Bible's great figures never did anything really serious at all.
Only if you hide it well; scripture keeps its heroes' worst moments out of the text.

notes: 'Denied Jesus three times' (fork) rests on Luke 22:34 and 22:61 ('thrice'); John 21:17 says 'the third time'. Confirm.
Psalm 51's heading links it to Nathan's visit after Bathsheba; the lesson says 'the heading ties that psalm to this moment' rather than asserting David's authorship as historical fact. Confirm.
Moses 'killed a man and ran to Midian' (Exodus 2:11–15): the text says he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew; the lesson keeps it brief. Keeper may want the context added.
'David's house suffered' summarizes 2 Samuel 12:10–14 and what follows; confirm.
howItsDone: 'in many liturgies' — soften if needed.
Audit: Peter 'promised', not 'swore', never to deny Jesus (Matthew 26:35, Luke 22:33); his swearing comes in the denial itself (Matthew 26:74).
